lines.text: How many numbers up to one thousand are multiples of four, six or nine?
lines.caption: How many numbers up to one thousand are multiples of four, six or nine?

lines.text: It's tempting to count each one and add. <short pause> But some numbers sneak in twice!
lines.caption: It's tempting to count each one and add. But some numbers sneak in twice!

lines.text: Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's count them carefully together.
lines.caption: Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's count them carefully together.

lines.text: Here's the question.
lines.caption: Here's the question.

lines.text: How many whole numbers from one to one thousand
lines.caption: How many whole numbers from one to one thousand

lines.text: are multiples of at least one of four, six and nine?
lines.caption: are multiples of at least one of four, six and nine?

lines.text: Here are the five choices. Take a good look.
lines.caption: Here are the five choices. Take a good look.

lines.text: So what are we counting? A number counts if four, six or nine goes into it.
lines.caption: So what are we counting? A number counts if four, six or nine goes into it.

lines.text: Just one is enough. Twelve fits two rules, four and six, but it counts only ONCE.
lines.caption: Just one is enough. Twelve fits two rules, four and six, but it counts only ONCE.

lines.text: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!
lines.caption: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

lines.text: Welcome back! First, let's count the multiples of each number on its own.
lines.caption: Welcome back! First, let's count the multiples of each number on its own.

lines.text: One thousand divided by four is two hundred fifty. That's two hundred fifty multiples of four.
lines.caption: One thousand divided by four is two hundred fifty. That's two hundred fifty multiples of four.

lines.text: One thousand divided by six is one hundred sixty-six, with four left over.
lines.caption: One thousand divided by six is one hundred sixty-six, with four left over.

lines.text: One thousand divided by nine is one hundred eleven, with one left over.
lines.caption: One thousand divided by nine is one hundred eleven, with one left over.

lines.text: Adding them gives five hundred twenty-seven. But wait, some numbers got counted twice!
lines.caption: Adding them gives five hundred twenty-seven. But wait, some numbers got counted twice!

lines.text: Twelve is a multiple of four AND six. So we counted it twice.
lines.caption: Twelve is a multiple of four AND six. So we counted it twice.

lines.text: Where do four and six meet? Four, eight, twelve. And six, twelve. They first meet at twelve.
lines.caption: Where do four and six meet? Four, eight, twelve. And six, twelve. They first meet at twelve.

lines.text: So the overlap is the multiples of twelve. Twenty-four would miss twelve and thirty-six!
lines.caption: So the overlap is the multiples of twelve. Twenty-four would miss twelve and thirty-six!

lines.text: Six and nine first meet at eighteen.
lines.caption: Six and nine first meet at eighteen.

lines.text: Four and nine share no factor except one. So they first meet at four times nine, thirty-six.
lines.caption: Four and nine share no factor except one. So they first meet at four times nine, thirty-six.

lines.text: Now divide by twelve, eighteen and thirty-six. We get eighty-three, fifty-five and twenty-seven.
lines.caption: Now divide by twelve, eighteen and thirty-six. We get eighty-three, fifty-five and twenty-seven.

lines.text: Eighty-three plus fifty-five plus twenty-seven is one hundred sixty-five. Let's take those away.
lines.caption: Eighty-three plus fifty-five plus twenty-seven is one hundred sixty-five. Let's take those away.

lines.text: Five hundred twenty-seven minus one hundred sixty-five,
lines.caption: Five hundred twenty-seven minus one hundred sixty-five,

lines.text: That is three hundred sixty-two. Are we done?
lines.caption: That is three hundred sixty-two. Are we done?

lines.text: Not yet! Think about thirty-six. It's a multiple of four, six AND nine.
lines.caption: Not yet! Think about thirty-six. It's a multiple of four, six AND nine.

lines.text: We counted it three times, then took it away three times. Now it's not counted at all!
lines.caption: We counted it three times, then took it away three times. Now it's not counted at all!

lines.text: All three first meet at thirty-six. So we add back those twenty-seven numbers, once.
lines.caption: All three first meet at thirty-six. So we add back those twenty-seven numbers, once.

lines.text: Three hundred sixty-two plus twenty-seven,
lines.caption: Three hundred sixty-two plus twenty-seven,

lines.text: That makes three hundred eighty-nine. The answer is C!
lines.caption: That makes three hundred eighty-nine. The answer is C!

lines.text: Here's something cool. Look at the slice for four and nine, without six.
lines.caption: Here's something cool. Look at the slice for four and nine, without six.

lines.text: A multiple of four and nine is a multiple of thirty-six. And thirty-six is a multiple of six!
lines.caption: A multiple of four and nine is a multiple of thirty-six. And thirty-six is a multiple of six!

lines.text: So that slice is empty. That's why the twenty-seven we took away came right back.
lines.caption: So that slice is empty. That's why the twenty-seven we took away came right back.

lines.text: Now for a second way. Let's build the list one rule at a time.
lines.caption: Now for a second way. Let's build the list one rule at a time.

lines.text: First, the multiples of four or six.
lines.caption: First, the multiples of four or six.

lines.text: Two hundred fifty plus one hundred sixty-six, minus eighty-three multiples of twelve.
lines.caption: Two hundred fifty plus one hundred sixty-six, minus eighty-three multiples of twelve.

lines.text: That's three hundred thirty-three so far. Now, which multiples of nine are NEW?
lines.caption: That's three hundred thirty-three so far. Now, which multiples of nine are NEW?

lines.text: An even multiple of nine is a multiple of eighteen. So it's a multiple of six, already counted.
lines.caption: An even multiple of nine is a multiple of eighteen. So it's a multiple of six, already counted.

lines.text: Multiples of four and six are all even. So every ODD multiple of nine is new.
lines.caption: Multiples of four and six are all even. So every ODD multiple of nine is new.

lines.text: There are one hundred eleven multiples of nine, and fifty-five are even. So fifty-six are odd.
lines.caption: There are one hundred eleven multiples of nine, and fifty-five are even. So fifty-six are odd.

lines.text: Three hundred thirty-three plus fifty-six is three hundred eighty-nine. Same answer!
lines.caption: Three hundred thirty-three plus fifty-six is three hundred eighty-nine. Same answer!

lines.text: When would you pick this way? When one overlap hides inside another, it saves steps.
lines.caption: When would you pick this way? When one overlap hides inside another, it saves steps.

lines.text: Now let's look at the wrong answers. Each one is a trap.
lines.caption: Now let's look at the wrong answers. Each one is a trap.

lines.text: Five hundred twenty-seven adds the three counts, but never takes away the overlaps.
lines.caption: Five hundred twenty-seven adds the three counts, but never takes away the overlaps.

lines.text: Three hundred sixty-two takes away the overlaps, but forgets to add the thirty-sixes back.
lines.caption: Three hundred sixty-two takes away the overlaps, but forgets to add the thirty-sixes back.

lines.text: Three hundred eighty-eight is what you'd get if you left out one thousand, a multiple of four!
lines.caption: Three hundred eighty-eight is what you'd get if you left out one thousand, a multiple of four!

lines.text: You'd get four hundred sixteen if you skipped four and nine, but added the thirty-sixes back.
lines.caption: You'd get four hundred sixteen if you skipped four and nine, but added the thirty-sixes back.

lines.text: Four and nine share no factor, but they still meet at thirty-six, seventy-two and more.
lines.caption: Four and nine share no factor, but they still meet at thirty-six, seventy-two and more.

lines.text: So here's a great habit. For each overlap, find the FIRST number where the two rules meet.
lines.caption: So here's a great habit. For each overlap, find the FIRST number where the two rules meet.

scenes.chapter: Four, six or ten: the answer

lines.text: Let's check. Three hundred divided by four, six and ten gives seventy-five, fifty and thirty.
lines.caption: Let's check. Three hundred divided by four, six and ten gives seventy-five, fifty and thirty.

lines.text: Adding those gives one hundred fifty-five.
lines.caption: Adding those gives one hundred fifty-five.

lines.text: The pairs first meet at twelve, twenty and thirty. That's twenty-five, fifteen and ten numbers.
lines.caption: The pairs first meet at twelve, twenty and thirty. That's twenty-five, fifteen and ten numbers.

lines.text: Take away those fifty. All three meet at sixty, and three hundred divided by sixty is five.
lines.caption: Take away those fifty. All three meet at sixty, and three hundred divided by sixty is five.

lines.text: So one hundred fifty-five minus fifty, plus five back,
lines.caption: So one hundred fifty-five minus fifty, plus five back,

lines.text: That makes one hundred ten! Amazing work!
lines.caption: That makes one hundred ten! Amazing work!

lines.text: Here's the big idea. Add the three counts. Take away each pair's overlap.
lines.caption: Here's the big idea. Add the three counts. Take away each pair's overlap.

lines.text: Then add back the overlap of all three.
lines.caption: Then add back the overlap of all three.

lines.text: For each overlap, use the smallest number they all go into. That's twelve, not twenty-four!
lines.caption: For each overlap, use the smallest number they all go into. That's twelve, not twenty-four!
